title: Indonesia’s new-home sales fall across all sizes while quoted prices still rise
summary: New-home sales in Bank Indonesia’s surveyed primary markets fell 8.43% in the third quarter from a year earlier, following a 2.36% decline in the second quarter. Developers still reported modest increases in prices. The residential property price index stood at 111.02, up 0.58% over the year and 0.11% over the quarter. Both rates were below the previous quarter’s 0.69% and 0.26%. The sharper deterioration was in the number of sales. A developer can experience weaker cash receipts before recording a fall in its quoted selling prices.

Large houses showed the most abrupt reversal. In the second quarter sales had been 13.08% above a year earlier. In the third they were 10.78% below. Medium properties had the steepest annual sales decline at 15.42%, following a 10.51% fall. Small homes fell 4.95% after a 2.88% decline. Quarterly sales fell 11.10%, reversing a 9.39% increase. The annual and quarterly series measure different changes, but both point to weaker turnover in the reporting period. They offer less information about the prices an existing homeowner would receive on resale.

On a quarter-on-quarter basis, large-unit sales fell 31.75% after rising 24.41%, while medium-unit sales fell 4.55% after a decline of 8.59%. Large houses thus experienced the sharper immediate reversal even though medium houses had the deepest annual contraction. The choice of comparison period changes which segment looks most exposed to a near-term interruption in collections.

The price indexes show meaningful differences within the market. Annual price growth slowed in seven of 18 surveyed cities. Yogyakarta recorded a 0.05% price decline after 0.77% growth, while price growth accelerated to 3.64% in Pekanbaru and 0.79% in Samarinda. Small homes registered 0.55% annual price growth after 0.49%, despite lower sales. These data concern primary residential property. The experience in the weakest city or size category cannot be carried across mechanically to an existing national mortgage portfolio.

The survey asked developers about the obstacles to sales. Building-material costs accounted for 26.24% of responses on constraints, licensing and bureaucracy for 17.17%, mortgage rates for 15.71%, taxes for 10.54% and large down payments for 10.05%. Mortgage rates were relatively stable compared with the second quarter. The results identify concerns among respondents. They do not estimate how many additional purchases would follow a particular change in rates, taxes or permit timing. Rising input costs could also put pressure on developers with little ability to raise selling prices.

The funding figures put that operating exposure in context. Developers financed 73.94% of their needs internally, 17.98% with bank loans and 8.08% with customer payments. Buyers used bank mortgages in 70.68% of purchase arrangements. These percentages describe different sides of a sale. Slower turnover can reach developers through lower receipts and lenders through reduced new mortgage business, without existing borrowers necessarily falling behind. Conversely, a rebound in sales and collections could improve liquidity before a price index shows a material increase. The report and its accompanying series allow the city- and size-level price changes to be checked separately from the volume and funding evidence.

questions.question: Would lower mortgage costs revive sales in the weakest categories?
questions.detail: Compare approvals, down-payment requirements and effective mortgage pricing by unit size and city. Track conversions from reservation to completion. If payments become more affordable but transactions remain weak, investigate construction delays or local demand before attributing the entire change to interest rates.

questions.question: Which developers can finance construction through a prolonged sales decline?
questions.detail: Reconcile receipts, buyer instalments, cash reserves and scheduled construction spending for each project. Track delivery dates and incentives as well as quoted prices. A developer can protect its price index through incentives while weakening both collections and margins.

questions.question: Do regional price changes signal broader deterioration in collateral?
questions.detail: Follow comparable size classes within the same cities using the data workbook. Distinguish the new-home price from available resale evidence and from forced-sale prices. Check whether the cities with slowing prices are also the locations where lenders have concentrated exposures.

questions.question: When does weak origination become a credit-performance problem?
questions.detail: Separate new approvals from repayment among existing mortgage cohorts. Track early arrears and loan modifications within the same region and borrower vintage. Falling origination with steady repayments primarily affects new business, whereas deterioration among established borrowers would change the credit assessment. Compare cohorts with the same seasoning.

limitation: The survey covers the primary market in 18 cities. Reported constraints and financing shares do not identify a causal effect of mortgage rates on sales.
